{{Short description|Concept in mathematics}}
In [[topology]] and related areas of [[mathematics]], the '''neighbourhood system''', '''complete system of neighbourhoods''',<ref>{{cite book|last=Mendelson|first=Bert|date=1990 |orig-year=1975|title=Introduction to Topology|edition=Third|publisher=Dover|isbn=0-486-66352-3|page=41}}</ref> or '''neighbourhood filter''' <math>\mathcal{N}(x)</math> for a point <math>x</math> in a [[topological space]] is the collection of all [[Neighbourhood (mathematics)|neighbourhood]]s of <math>x.</math>

==Definitions==

'''Neighbourhood of a point or set'''

An {{em|{{visible anchor|open neighbourhood}}}} of a point (or [[subset]]<ref group=note name=nhoodOfPointVsSet />) <math>x</math> in a topological space <math>X</math> is any [[Open set|open subset]] <math>U</math> of <math>X</math> that contains <math>x.</math>
A {{em|{{visible anchor|neighbourhood}} of <math>x</math> in <math>X</math>}} is any subset <math>N \subseteq X</math> that contains {{em|some}} open neighbourhood of <math>x</math>; 
explicitly, <math>N</math> is a neighbourhood of <math>x</math> in <math>X</math> [[if and only if]] there exists some open subset <math>U</math> with <math>x \in U \subseteq N</math>.{{sfn|Bourbaki|1989|pp=17-21}}{{sfn|Willard|2004|pp=31-37}} 
Equivalently, a neighborhood of <math>x</math> is any set that contains <math>x</math> in its [[interior (topology)|topological interior]].

Importantly, a "neighbourhood" does {{em|not}} have to be an open set; those neighbourhoods that also happen to be open sets are known as "open neighbourhoods."<ref group=note name=NhoodsNotRequiredToBeOpen /> 
Similarly, a neighbourhood that is also a [[Closed set|closed]] (respectively, [[compact space|compact]], [[connected space|connected]], etc.) set is called a {{em|{{visible anchor|closed neighbourhood}}}} (respectively, {{em|{{visible anchor|compact neighbourhood}}}}, {{em|{{visible anchor|connected neighbourhood}}}}, etc.). 
There are many other types of neighbourhoods that are used in topology and related fields like [[functional analysis]]. 
The family of all neighbourhoods having a certain "useful" property often forms a [[#neighbourhood basis|neighbourhood basis]], although many times, these neighbourhoods are not necessarily open. [[Locally compact space]]s, for example, are those spaces that, at every point, have a neighbourhood basis consisting entirely of compact sets. 

'''Neighbourhood filter'''

The neighbourhood system for a point (or [[empty set|non-empty]] subset) <math>x</math> is a [[Filter on a set|filter]] called the {{em|neighbourhood filter for <math>x.</math>}} The neighbourhood filter for a point <math>x \in X</math> is the same as the neighbourhood filter of the [[singleton set]] <math>\{x\}.</math>

===Neighbourhood basis===

A {{em|{{visible anchor|neighbourhood basis}}}} or {{em|{{visible anchor|local basis}}}} (or {{em|{{visible anchor|neighbourhood base}}}} or {{em|{{visible anchor|local base}}}}) for a point <math>x</math> is a [[filter base]] of the neighbourhood filter; this means that it is a subset
<math display=block>\mathcal{B} \subseteq \mathcal{N}(x)</math>such that for all <math>V \in \mathcal{N}(x),</math> there exists some <math>B \in \mathcal{B}</math> such that <math>B \subseteq V.</math>{{sfn|Willard|2004|pp=31-37}} Here, <math>\mathcal{N}(x)</math> denotes the set of all neighbourhoods of <math>x</math>. That is, for any neighbourhood <math>V</math> we can find a neighbourhood <math>B</math> in the neighbourhood basis that is contained in <math>V.</math>

Equivalently, <math>\mathcal{B}</math> is a local basis at <math>x</math> if and only if the neighbourhood filter <math>\mathcal{N}</math> can be recovered from <math>\mathcal{B}</math> in the sense that the following equality holds:<ref>{{cite book|last=Willard|first=Stephen|date=1970|title=General Topology |url=https://archive.org/details/generaltopology00will_0|url-access=registration|publisher=Addison-Wesley Publishing|isbn=9780201087079}} (See Chapter 2, Section 4)</ref><math display=block>\mathcal{N}(x) = \left\{ V \subseteq X ~:~ B \subseteq V \text{ for some } B \in \mathcal{B} \right\}\!\!\;.</math> A family <math>\mathcal{B} \subseteq \mathcal{N}(x)</math> is a neighbourhood basis for <math>x</math> if and only if <math>\mathcal{B}</math> is a [[Cofinal set|cofinal subset]] of <math>\left(\mathcal{N}(x), \supseteq\right)</math> with respect to the [[partial order]] <math>\supseteq</math> (importantly, this partial order is the [[superset]] relation and not the [[subset]] relation).

===Neighbourhood subbasis===

A {{em|{{visible anchor|neighbourhood subbasis}}}} at <math>x</math> is a family <math>\mathcal{S}</math> of subsets of <math>X,</math> each of which contains <math>x,</math> such that the collection of all possible finite [[intersection (set theory)|intersections]] of elements of <math>\mathcal{S}</math> forms a neighbourhood basis at <math>x.</math>

==Examples==

If <math>\R</math> has its usual [[Euclidean topology]] then the neighborhoods of <math>0</math> are all those subsets <math>N \subseteq \R</math> for which there exists some [[real number]] <math>r > 0</math> such that <math>(-r, r) \subseteq N.</math> For example, all of the following sets are neighborhoods of <math>0</math> in <math>\R</math>:
<math display=block>(-2, 2), \; [-2,2], \; [-2, \infty), \; [-2, 2) \cup \{10\}, \; [-2, 2] \cup \Q, \; \R</math>
but none of the following sets are neighborhoods  of <math>0</math>: 
<math display=block>\{0\}, \; \Q, \; (0,2), \; [0, 2), \; [0, 2) \cup \Q, \; (-2, 2) \setminus \left\{1, \tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{1}{3}, \tfrac{1}{4}, \ldots\right\}</math> 
where <math>\Q</math> denotes the [[rational number]]s. 

If <math>U</math> is an open subset of a [[topological space]] <math>X</math> then for every <math>u \in U,</math> <math>U</math> is a neighborhood of <math>u</math> in <math>X.</math> 
More generally, if <math>N \subseteq X</math> is any set and <math>\operatorname{int}_X N</math> denotes the [[interior (topology)|topological interior]] of <math>N</math> in <math>X,</math> then <math>N</math> is a neighborhood (in <math>X</math>) of every point <math>x \in \operatorname{int}_X N</math> and moreover, <math>N</math> is {{em|not}} a neighborhood of any other point. 
Said differently, <math>N</math> is a neighborhood of a point <math>x \in X</math> if and only if <math>x \in \operatorname{int}_X N.</math>

'''Neighbourhood bases'''

In any topological space, the neighbourhood system for a point is also a neighbourhood basis for the point. The set of all open neighbourhoods at a point forms a neighbourhood basis at that point. 
For any point <math>x</math> in a [[metric space]], the sequence of [[open ball]]s around <math>x</math> with radius <math>1/n</math> form a [[countable]] neighbourhood basis <math>\mathcal{B} = \left\{B_{1/n} : n = 1,2,3,\dots \right\}</math>. This means every metric space is [[first-countable]].

Given a space <math>X</math> with the [[indiscrete topology]] the neighbourhood system for any point <math>x</math> only contains the whole space, <math>\mathcal{N}(x) = \{X\}</math>.

In the [[weak topology]] on the space of measures on a space <math>E,</math> a neighbourhood base about <math>\nu</math> is given by
<math display=block>\left\{\mu \in \mathcal{M}(E) : \left|\mu f_i - \nu f_i\right| < r_i, \, i = 1,\dots,n\right\}</math>
where <math>f_i</math> are [[continuous function (topology)|continuous]] bounded functions from <math>E</math> to the real numbers and <math>r_1, \dots, r_n</math> are positive real numbers.

'''Seminormed spaces and topological groups'''

In a [[seminormed space]], that is a [[vector space]] with the [[topological space|topology]] induced by a [[seminorm]], all neighbourhood systems can be constructed by [[Translation (geometry)|translation]] of the neighbourhood system for the origin,
<math display=block>\mathcal{N}(x) = \mathcal{N}(0) + x.</math>

This is because, by assumption, vector addition is separately continuous in the induced topology. Therefore, the topology is determined by its neighbourhood system at the origin. More generally, this remains true whenever the space is a [[topological group]] or the topology is defined by a [[Pseudometric space|pseudometric]].

==Properties==

Suppose <math>u \in U \subseteq X</math> and let <math>\mathcal{N}</math> be a neighbourhood basis for <math>u</math> in <math>X.</math> Make <math>\mathcal{N}</math> into a [[directed set]] by [[partial order|partially ordering]] it by superset inclusion <math>\,\supseteq.</math> Then <math>U</math> is {{em|not}} a neighborhood of <math>u</math> in <math>X</math> if and only if there exists an <math>\mathcal{N}</math>-indexed [[net (mathematics)|net]] <math>\left(x_N\right)_{N \in \mathcal{N}}</math> in <math>X \setminus U</math> such that <math>x_N \in N \setminus U</math> for every <math>N \in \mathcal{N}</math> (which implies that <math>\left(x_N\right)_{N \in \mathcal{N}} \to u</math> in <math>X</math>).

==References==

{{reflist|group=note|refs=
<ref group=note name=nhoodOfPointVsSet>Usually, "neighbourhood" refers to a neighbourhood {{em|of a point}} and it will be clearly indicated if it instead refers to a neighborhood of a set. 
So for instance, a statement such as "a neighbourhood in <math>X</math>" that does not refer to any particular point or set should, unless somehow indicated otherwise, be taken to mean "a neighbourhood {{em|of some point}} in <math>X.</math>"</ref>

<ref group=note name=NhoodsNotRequiredToBeOpen>Most authors do not require that neighborhoods be open sets because writing "open" in front of "neighborhood" when this property is needed is not overly onerous and because requiring that they always be open would also greatly limit the usefulness of terms such as "closed neighborhood" and "compact neighborhood".</ref>
}}
{{reflist}}
